section.title: The Chomsky Hierarchy and the Boundary of Constructibility
section.para: The Chomsky hierarchy classifies formal languages — and hence sets such as Th(T) — by the class of automaton required to recognise them.

Types 1 through 3 are all recursive: recognition by a linear-bounded automaton, a pushdown automaton, or a finite automaton is always a total procedure that terminates in finite time. Type 0 captures the recursively enumerable sets; a Type 0 language may not be recursive, and its membership problem may be only semi-decidable.
Whether Th(T) for a given theory T falls at or below the recursive boundary determines what kind of computational witness can be constructed:

listitem.para: If Th(T) is recursive, a decider (as defined in the preceding section) witnesses the decision problem of T.
If Th(T) is properly RE (RE but not recursive), only a semi-decider can be constructed; no decider exists.
If Th(T) is not RE, no Turing-machine witness of either kind exists.

section.para: This library witnesses specific named theories whose membership in one of these three classes has a known, positive resolution. It does not witness the set of all first-order theories: that set is not computably characterised. It contains True Arithmetic — Th(ℕ, +, ×, 0, 1) under the standard model — which is not arithmetically definable, as well as essentially undecidable theories such as Robinson arithmetic Q, for which no consistent extension is decidable. Membership in the set of all first-order theories therefore admits no general decision procedure, classical or otherwise.
